case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented with a chronic, painful, nonhealing ulcer on her fifth finger that developed after trauma 1 year earlier (Figure 1A). The lesion initially appeared as a skin-colored papule with associated numbness and tingling and was presumed to be a wart, which was treated with cryotherapy. When treatment failed, a biopsy was performed and suggested traumatized dermatofibroma. Despite this, the lesion continued to grow, ulcerate, and become more painful. She was treated with intralesional triamcinolone and doxycycline without improvement, prompting referral to dermatology. On examination, her PARACELSUS score was greater than 10, suggesting the possible diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Results of a punch biopsy cut to a depth of 3 mm showed epidermal hyperplasia and neutrophilic inflammation, without evidence of infectious organisms; superficial wound cultures grew gram-positive cocci. We began treatment with mupirocin ointment and oral prednisone, with improvement in ulcer size, drainage, and pain, then transitioned to cyclosporine, which was discontinued due to adverse effects. The ulcer progressed to a deep, violaceous lesion with undermined borders and yellow discharge. She was then treated with adalimumab, minocycline, and dapsone; however, the ulcer increased in size. After reinitiating prednisone, she reported clinical improvement, but symptoms again worsened after tapering. Radiology demonstrated soft tissue swelling but no bony necrosis. Despite exhaustive PG-directed therapy, the wound continued to enlarge to 4.5 × 3.0 cm, exposing tendon, with increased drainage and pain, prompting evaluation with point-of-care high-frequency ultrasonography (HFUS) and repeat biopsy (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Fifth digit ulceration with raised, erythematous borders and drainage on initial dermatology visit. B, Poorly circumscribed infiltrate of atypical epithelioid cells within the dermis dissecting between collagen bundles with mixed inflammatory infiltrate. Epithelioid cells have round to oval, enlarged nuclei with vesicular chromatin, some pleomorphic, and abundant amphophilic cytoplasm.
case_info.explanation: Histopathology results revealed an atypical epithelioid proliferation with positive staining for pancytokeratin, CD34, and ERG, with patchy CD31 positivity. There was negative staining for CD68, SOX10, S100 protein, human herpesvirus 8, calponin, p63, CK7, and CK20. Notably, there was loss of INI1 expression and no bacteria (Gram stain), fungi (periodic acid–Schiff stain), or acid-fast bacilli (Fite stain) were identified. Results of pathology, immunostaining, and imaging (Figure 2) confirmed the diagnosis of classic-type epithelioid sarcoma (ES). Immunosuppressants were discontinued, and the patient was referred to a multidisciplinary sarcoma team, ultimately requiring amputation. ES is a rare soft-tissue neoplasm most commonly affecting the distal extremities of young adults, with peak incidence around the age of 35 years.1It tends to grow along tendons, fascia, and nerves, with differentiation reflected in its varied immunohistochemical findings.2Histologically, ES appears as a dermal or subcutaneous nodule composed of epithelioid and spindle cells, which may be well circumscribed or irregularly lobulated, often with central necrosis. Immunohistochemistry typically shows positive results for cytokeratin and vimentin, with approximately 50% of cases with positive staining for CD34 and 40% showing ERG immunoreactivity.3,4ES is usually negative for S100, desmin, FLI-1, and CD31, although focal CD31 cytoplasmic expression has been described.2,5The highly sensitive diagnostic feature is loss of nuclear SMARCB1/INI1 protein expression.1 Prognosis remains poor due to diagnostic delays, high local recurrence rates, and distant metastasis. Five-year survival ranges from 25% to 70%.1The proximal subtype, typically involving the trunk, pelvis, or proximal limbs, is characterized by larger, pleomorphic cells and follows a more aggressive course.1The more common classic (distal) subtype typically affects the hands and forearms and may initially be less aggressive; however, it can metastasize, and the presence of high-grade histologic features, such as mitoses, necrosis, and atypia, results in behavior resembling the proximal variant. Importantly, ES is often chemoresistant, which explains why radical surgical approaches, including amputation in this case, may be required.1 Clinically, ES initially presents as a painless, firm dermal or subcutaneous nodule. It has been associated with prior trauma and may develop superficial bleeding or necrosis that can become painful.1Rarely, ES manifests as a nonhealing, ulcerative process with raised margins, mimicking conditions like perforating granuloma annulare,Mycobacterium ulcerans, or even PG, as in a case where diagnosis was delayed for 18 years.6Distinguishing features include the histologic absence of palisading granulomas, lack of organisms, and confirmatory immunohistochemical findings. Given the ambiguous presentation of ES, accurate diagnosis requires a high level of suspicion. HFUS has successfully identified ES even when tumors were not palpable or initially missed with magnetic resonance imaging, and it is increasingly used in skin oncology to assess lesion depth and vascularization.7,8Contrary to ES, findings of HFUS for perforating granuloma annulare typically appear as a poorly defined hypoechoic band in the dermis, while active PG demonstrates a heterogeneous, edematous process.9,10When used alongside clinical assessment and dermatopathology, HFUS can help differentiate lesions and assess involvement with nearby structures. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge in distinguishing ES from mimicking ulcers and emphasizes the importance of early imaging and repeat biopsy with immunohistochemical staining to reduce morbidity and guide appropriate treatment.

A woman in her mid-70s with a medical history of coronary artery disease (CAD) and left anterior descending artery stenting complained of unexplained dyspnea on exertion. An exercise transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted by the referring cardiologist as part of the CAD follow-up, which resulted in an end-test uncontrollable cough with acute dyspnea. Coronary angiography was performed and showed no evidence of ischemic progression. Subsequent pulmonary evaluations, including respiratory functional assessments, walking tests, and thoracic computed tomography scans, yielded normal results. The patient was therefore referred to the university hospital. Upon arrival at the specialized cardiology consultation, the patient exhibited an anxious state associated with tachycardia and the same dyspnea. The initial TTE demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with notable tenting and the absence of valve coaptation (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved at 70%, without any wall-motion abnormality, no LV dilation, and preserved global longitudinal strain of −21%. The electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block (LBBB). As the examination continued, the heart rate decreased, accompanied by the disappearance of the symptoms. TTE subsequently demonstrated regression of the MR, which became minimal, without any tenting (Figure 1B), while the ECG exhibited narrowing of the QRS complexes. These findings were confirmed by an exercise TTE, which rapidly showed recurrence of LBBB and severe MR, followed by acute dyspnea and multiple B lines at lung ultrasound.

Case:
A 24-year-old man presented with progressive gait instability. Although this started in childhood as a tendency to drag his left leg and trip, he could keep his balance on a skateboard until the age of 14 years. He had no significant medical history. There was neither family history of neurological illnesses nor consanguinity. Upon neurologic examination, he had normal cognition, slight dysarthria, impaired smooth pursuit, subtle tremor of both hands, left-sided spasticity, normal muscle strength, mildly impaired joint position sense in his toes bilaterally, and hyperreflexia with increased patellar and ankle jerk reflexes. Pes cavus and Babinski sign were present bilaterally as well as truncal and appendicular ataxia. Several teeth were absent (hypodontia) or too small (microdontia). Electrocardiogram results were normal. Complete blood cell count, thyroid, liver, and kidney function were within normal limits. A magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the brain and upper spinal cord (Figure 1) showed marked spinal cord atrophy with an anterior-posterior width of 4 mm, isolated hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles, and atrophy of the isthmus of the corpus callosum.

Sagittal fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) (A) and T1-weighted imaging (B) of the brain and upper spinal cord showing marked spinal cord atrophy (A and B, pink arrowhead), isolated hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncle (A, blue arrowhead), and atrophy of the isthmus of the corpus callosum (B, blue arrowhead).

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

[Conversation so far]

Therefore, the most appropriate next step is to initiate a referral to a neurologist specializing in movement disorders or neurogenetics for confirmatory genetic testing and comprehensive long-term management planning.

However, the specific MRI pattern of isolated superior cerebellar peduncle hyperintensity, spinal cord atrophy, and hypodontia points strongly towards a diagnosis of autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (ARSACS). The next step would indeed be SACS gene testing to confirm.

Case:
A 61-year-old man presented with chronic progressive weakness and gait dysfunction. Four years prior, he developed progressive arm and leg weakness. He subsequently experienced recurrent falls, attributed to gait imbalance and tripping over his feet, and urinary incontinence. One year prior, his wife noted progressive memory loss (eg, getting lost when going to familiar places), dysarthria, and episodes of inappropriate laughter (ie, involuntarily laughing without a clear emotional trigger). He had a history of hypertension. There was no known history of a neurological disorder in his family. He had Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry in his maternal lineage. There was no known consanguinity. Neurological examination revealed impaired short-term recall (recalled 0 of 5 words at 5 minutes) and a pseudobulbar affect. His cranial nerve examination was notable for a spastic dysarthria without tongue atrophy/fasciculations. There was upper and lower extremity spasticity, atrophy of intrinsic hand and calf muscles, and mild weakness of his intrinsic hand and distal lower extremity muscles bilaterally. There was decreased large-fiber sensation distally in his lower extremities. Romberg sign was absent. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ at the biceps and patellars and absent at the ankles. Plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Cerebellar function was normal. The gait was spastic. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed confluent T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter involving the corticospinal tracts, posterior limb of internal capsule, external capsule, and medial lemniscus and corticospinal tracts at the pons and medulla (Figure). There was negative staining for CD68, SOX10, S100 protein, human herpesvirus 8, calponin, p63, CK7, and CK20. Notably, there was loss of INI1 expression and no bacteria (Gram stain), fungi (periodic acid–Schiff stain), or acid-fast bacilli (Fite stain) were identified. Results of pathology, immunostaining, and imaging (Figure 2) confirmed the diagnosis of classic-type epithelioid sarcoma (ES). Immunosuppressants were discontinued, and the patient was referred to a multidisciplinary sarcoma team, ultimately requiring amputation. ES is a rare soft-tissue neoplasm most commonly affecting the distal extremities of young adults, with peak incidence around the age of 35 years.1It tends to grow along tendons, fascia, and nerves, with differentiation reflected in its varied immunohistochemical findings.2Histologically, ES appears as a dermal or subcutaneous nodule composed of epithelioid and spindle cells, which may be well circumscribed or irregularly lobulated, often with central necrosis. Immunohistochemistry typically shows positive results for cytokeratin and vimentin, with approximately 50% of cases with positive staining for CD34 and 40% showing ERG immunoreactivity.3,4ES is usually negative for S100, desmin, FLI-1, and CD31, although focal CD31 cytoplasmic expression has been described.2,5The highly sensitive diagnostic feature is loss of nuclear SMARCB1/INI1 protein expression.1 Prognosis remains poor due to diagnostic delays, high local recurrence rates, and distant metastasis. Five-year survival ranges from 25% to 70%.1The proximal subtype, typically involving the trunk, pelvis, or proximal limbs, is characterized by larger, pleomorphic cells and follows a more aggressive course.1The more common classic (distal) subtype typically affects the hands and forearms and may initially be less aggressive; however, it can metastasize, and the presence of high-grade histologic features, such as mitoses, necrosis, and atypia, results in behavior resembling the proximal variant. Importantly, ES is often chemoresistant, which explains why radical surgical approaches, including amputation in this case, may be required.1 Clinically, ES initially presents as a painless, firm dermal or subcutaneous nodule. It has been associated with prior trauma and may develop superficial bleeding or necrosis that can become painful.1Rarely, ES manifests as a nonhealing, ulcerative process with raised margins, mimicking conditions like perforating granuloma annulare,Mycobacterium ulcerans, or even PG, as in a case where diagnosis was delayed for 18 years.6Distinguishing features include the histologic absence of palisading granulomas, lack of organisms, and confirmatory immunohistochemical findings. Given the ambiguous presentation of ES, accurate diagnosis requires a high level of suspicion. HFUS has successfully identified ES even when tumors were not palpable or initially missed with magnetic resonance imaging, and it is increasingly used in skin oncology to assess lesion depth and vascularization.7,8Contrary to ES, findings of HFUS for perforating granuloma annulare typically appear as a poorly defined hypoechoic band in the dermis, while active PG demonstrates a heterogeneous, edematous process.9,10When used alongside clinical assessment and dermatopathology, HFUS can help differentiate lesions and assess involvement with nearby structures. case_info.explanation: Histopathology results revealed an atypical epithelioid proliferation with positive staining for pancytokeratin, CD34, and ERG, with patchy CD31 positivity. There was negative staining for CD68, SOX10, S100 protein, human herpesvirus 8, calponin, p63, CK7, and CK20. Notably, there was loss of INI1 expression and no bacteria (Gram stain), fungi (periodic acid–Schiff stain), or acid-fast bacilli (Fite stain) were identified. Results of pathology, immunostaining, and imaging (Figure 2) confirmed the diagnosis of classic-type epithelioid sarcoma (ES). Immunosuppressants were discontinued, and the patient was referred to a multidisciplinary sarcoma team, ultimately requiring amputation. ES is a rare soft-tissue neoplasm most commonly affecting the distal extremities of young adults, with peak incidence around the age of 35 years.1It tends to grow along tendons, fascia, and nerves, with differentiation reflected in its varied immunohistochemical findings.2Histologically, ES appears as a dermal or subcutaneous nodule composed of epithelioid and spindle cells, which may be well circumscribed or irregularly lobulated, often with central necrosis. Immunohistochemistry typically shows positive results for cytokeratin and vimentin, with approximately 50% of cases with positive staining for CD34 and 40% showing ERG immunoreactivity.3,4ES is usually negative for S100, desmin, FLI-1, and CD31, although focal CD31 cytoplasmic expression has been described.2,5The highly sensitive diagnostic feature is loss of nuclear SMARCB1/INI1 protein expression.1 Prognosis remains poor due to diagnostic delays, high local recurrence rates, and distant metastasis. Five-year survival ranges from 25% to 70%.1The proximal subtype, typically involving the trunk, pelvis, or proximal limbs, is characterized by larger, pleomorphic cells and follows a more aggressive course.1The more common classic (distal) subtype typically affects the hands and forearms and may initially be less aggressive; however, it can metastasize, and the presence of high-grade histologic features, such as mitoses, necrosis, and atypia, results in behavior resembling the proximal variant. Importantly, ES is often chemoresistant, which explains why radical surgical approaches, including amputation in this case, may be required.1 Clinically, ES initially presents as a painless, firm dermal or subcutaneous nodule. It has been associated with prior trauma and may develop superficial bleeding or necrosis that can become painful.1Rarely, ES manifests as a nonhealing, ulcerative process with raised margins, mimicking conditions like perforating granuloma annulare,Mycobacterium ulcerans, or even PG, as in a case where diagnosis was delayed for 18 years.6Distinguishing features include the histologic absence of palisading granulomas, lack of organisms, and confirmatory immunohistochemical findings. Given the ambiguous presentation of ES, accurate diagnosis requires a high level of suspicion. HFUS has successfully identified ES even when tumors were not palpable or initially missed with magnetic resonance imaging, and it is increasingly used in skin oncology to assess lesion depth and vascularization.7,8Contrary to ES, findings of HFUS for perforating granuloma annulare typically appear as a poorly defined hypoechoic band in the dermis, while active PG demonstrates a heterogeneous, edematous process.9,10When used alongside clinical assessment and dermatopathology, HFUS can help differentiate lesions and assess involvement with nearby structures. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge in distinguishing ES from mimicking ulcers and emphasizes the importance of early imaging and repeat biopsy with immunohistochemical staining to reduce morbidity and guide appropriate treatment.

A 61-year-old man presented with chronic progressive weakness and gait dysfunction. Four years prior, he developed progressive arm and leg weakness. He subsequently experienced recurrent falls, attributed to gait imbalance and tripping over his feet, and urinary incontinence. One year prior, his wife noted progressive memory loss (eg, getting lost when going to familiar places), dysarthria, and episodes of inappropriate laughter (ie, involuntarily laughing without a clear emotional trigger). He had a history of hypertension. There was no known history of a neurological disorder in his family. He had Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry in his maternal lineage. There was no known consanguinity. Neurological examination revealed impaired short-term recall (recalled 0 of 5 words at 5 minutes) and a pseudobulbar affect. His cranial nerve examination was notable for a spastic dysarthria without tongue atrophy/fasciculations. There was upper and lower extremity spasticity, atrophy of intrinsic hand and calf muscles, and mild weakness of his intrinsic hand and distal lower extremity muscles bilaterally. There was decreased large-fiber sensation distally in his lower extremities. Romberg sign was absent. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ at the biceps and patellars and absent at the ankles. Plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Cerebellar function was normal. The gait was spastic. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed confluent T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter involving the corticospinal tracts, posterior limb of internal capsule, external capsule, and medial lemniscus and corticospinal tracts at the pons and medulla (Figure). MRI of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord showed diffuse atrophy without signal abnormalities. Electromyography revealed a chronic sensorimotor axonal neuropathy and lumbosacral radiculopathies. He had normal levels of vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, copper, vitamin E, lactate/pyruvate, very long chain fatty acids, plasma/urine amino acids, and lysosomal enzymes, a normal bile acids profile, and negative infectious serologies (HIV, syphilis, and human T-lymphotropic virus). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell counts, protein and glucose levels, oligoclonal band profile, and IgG index.

A woman in her mid-70s with a medical history of coronary artery disease (CAD) and left anterior descending artery stenting complained of unexplained dyspnea on exertion. An exercise transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted by the referring cardiologist as part of the CAD follow-up, which resulted in an end-test uncontrollable cough with acute dyspnea. Coronary angiography was performed and showed no evidence of ischemic progression. Subsequent pulmonary evaluations, including respiratory functional assessments, walking tests, and thoracic computed tomography scans, yielded normal results. The patient was therefore referred to the university hospital. Upon arrival at the specialized cardiology consultation, the patient exhibited an anxious state associated with tachycardia and the same dyspnea. The initial TTE demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with notable tenting and the absence of valve coaptation (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved at 70%, without any wall-motion abnormality, no LV dilation, and preserved global longitudinal strain of −21%. The electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block (LBBB). As the examination continued, the heart rate decreased, accompanied by the disappearance of the symptoms. TTE subsequently demonstrated regression of the MR, which became minimal, without any tenting (Figure 1B), while the ECG exhibited narrowing of the QRS complexes. These findings were confirmed by an exercise TTE, which rapidly showed recurrence of LBBB and severe MR, followed by acute dyspnea and multiple B lines at lung ultrasound.

Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). A woman in her 30s presented with a chronic, painful, nonhealing ulcer on her fifth finger that developed after trauma 1 year earlier (Figure 1A). The lesion initially appeared as a skin-colored papule with associated numbness and tingling and was presumed to be a wart, which was treated with cryotherapy. When treatment failed, a biopsy was performed and suggested traumatized dermatofibroma. Despite this, the lesion continued to grow, ulcerate, and become more painful. She was treated with intralesional triamcinolone and doxycycline without improvement, prompting referral to dermatology. On examination, her PARACELSUS score was greater than 10, suggesting the possible diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Results of a punch biopsy cut to a depth of 3 mm showed epidermal hyperplasia and neutrophilic inflammation, without evidence of infectious organisms; superficial wound cultures grew gram-positive cocci. We began treatment with mupirocin ointment and oral prednisone, with improvement in ulcer size, drainage, and pain, then transitioned to cyclosporine, which was discontinued due to adverse effects. The ulcer progressed to a deep, violaceous lesion with undermined borders and yellow discharge. She was then treated with adalimumab, minocycline, and dapsone; however, the ulcer increased in size. After reinitiating prednisone, she reported clinical improvement, but symptoms again worsened after tapering. Radiology demonstrated soft tissue swelling but no bony necrosis. Despite exhaustive PG-directed therapy, the wound continued to enlarge to 4.5 × 3.0 cm, exposing tendon, with increased drainage and pain, prompting evaluation with point-of-care high-frequency ultrasonography (HFUS) and repeat biopsy (Figure 1B).

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented with a chronic, painful, nonhealing ulcer on her fifth finger that developed after trauma 1 year earlier (Figure 1A). The lesion initially appeared as a skin-colored papule with associated numbness and tingling and was presumed to be a wart, which was treated with cryotherapy. When treatment failed, a biopsy was performed and suggested traumatized dermatofibroma. Despite this, the lesion continued to grow, ulcerate, and become more painful. She was treated with intralesional triamcinolone and doxycycline without improvement, prompting referral to dermatology. On examination, her PARACELSUS score was greater than 10, suggesting the possible diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Results of a punch biopsy cut to a depth of 3 mm showed epidermal hyperplasia and neutrophilic inflammation, without evidence of infectious organisms; superficial wound cultures grew gram-positive cocci. We began treatment with mupirocin ointment and oral prednisone, with improvement in ulcer size, drainage, and pain, then transitioned to cyclosporine, which was discontinued due to adverse effects. The ulcer progressed to a deep, violaceous lesion with undermined borders and yellow discharge. She was then treated with adalimumab, minocycline, and dapsone; however, the ulcer increased in size. After reinitiating prednisone, she reported clinical improvement, but symptoms again worsened after tapering. Radiology demonstrated soft tissue swelling but no bony necrosis. Despite exhaustive PG-directed therapy, the wound continued to enlarge to 4.5 × 3.0 cm, exposing tendon, with increased drainage and pain, prompting evaluation with point-of-care high-frequency ultrasonography (HFUS) and repeat biopsy (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Fifth digit ulceration with raised, erythematous borders and drainage on initial dermatology visit. B, Poorly circumscribed infiltrate of atypical epithelioid cells within the dermis dissecting between collagen bundles with mixed inflammatory infiltrate. Epithelioid cells have round to oval, enlarged nuclei with vesicular chromatin, some pleomorphic, and abundant amphophilic cytoplasm.
case_info.explanation: Histopathology results revealed an atypical epithelioid proliferation with positive staining for pancytokeratin, CD34, and ERG, with patchy CD31 positivity. There was negative staining for CD68, SOX10, S100 protein, human herpesvirus 8, calponin, p63, CK7, and CK20. Notably, there was loss of INI1 expression and no bacteria (Gram stain), fungi (periodic acid–Schiff stain), or acid-fast bacilli (Fite stain) were identified. Results of pathology, immunostaining, and imaging (Figure 2) confirmed the diagnosis of classic-type epithelioid sarcoma (ES). Immunosuppressants were discontinued, and the patient was referred to a multidisciplinary sarcoma team, ultimately requiring amputation. ES is a rare soft-tissue neoplasm most commonly affecting the distal extremities of young adults, with peak incidence around the age of 35 years.1It tends to grow along tendons, fascia, and nerves, with differentiation reflected in its varied immunohistochemical findings.2Histologically, ES appears as a dermal or subcutaneous nodule composed of epithelioid and spindle cells, which may be well circumscribed or irregularly lobulated, often with central necrosis. Immunohistochemistry typically shows positive results for cytokeratin and vimentin, with approximately 50% of cases with positive staining for CD34 and 40% showing ERG immunoreactivity.3,4ES is usually negative for S100, desmin, FLI-1, and CD31, although focal CD31 cytoplasmic expression has been described.2,5The highly sensitive diagnostic feature is loss of nuclear SMARCB1/INI1 protein expression.1 Prognosis remains poor due to diagnostic delays, high local recurrence rates, and distant metastasis. Five-year survival ranges from 25% to 70%.1The proximal subtype, typically involving the trunk, pelvis, or proximal limbs, is characterized by larger, pleomorphic cells and follows a more aggressive course.1The more common classic (distal) subtype typically affects the hands and forearms and may initially be less aggressive; however, it can metastasize, and the presence of high-grade histologic features, such as mitoses, necrosis, and atypia, results in behavior resembling the proximal variant. Importantly, ES is often chemoresistant, which explains why radical surgical approaches, including amputation in this case, may be required.1 Clinically, ES initially presents as a painless, firm dermal or subcutaneous nodule. It has been associated with prior trauma and may develop superficial bleeding or necrosis that can become painful.1Rarely, ES manifests as a nonhealing, ulcerative process with raised margins, mimicking conditions like perforating granuloma annulare,Mycobacterium ulcerans, or even PG, as in a case where diagnosis was delayed for 18 years.6Distinguishing features include the histologic absence of palisading granulomas, lack of organisms, and confirmatory immunohistochemical findings. Given the ambiguous presentation of ES, accurate diagnosis requires a high level of suspicion. HFUS has successfully identified ES even when tumors were not palpable or initially missed with magnetic resonance imaging, and it is increasingly used in skin oncology to assess lesion depth and vascularization.7,8Contrary to ES, findings of HFUS for perforating granuloma annulare typically appear as a poorly defined hypoechoic band in the dermis, while active PG demonstrates a heterogeneous, edematous process.9,10When used alongside clinical assessment and dermatopathology, HFUS can help differentiate lesions and assess involvement with nearby structures. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge in distinguishing ES from mimicking ulcers and emphasizes the importance of early imaging and repeat biopsy with immunohistochemical staining to reduce morbidity and guide appropriate treatment.

case_info.explanation: Histopathology results revealed an atypical epithelioid proliferation with positive staining for pancytokeratin, CD34, and ERG, with patchy CD31 positivity. There was negative staining for CD68, SOX10, S100 protein, human herpesvirus 8, calponin, p63, CK7, and CK20. Notably, there was loss of INI1 expression and no bacteria (Gram stain), fungi (periodic acid–Schiff stain), or acid-fast bacilli (Fite stain) were identified. Results of pathology, immunostaining, and imaging (Figure 2) confirmed the diagnosis of classic-type epithelioid sarcoma (ES). Immunosuppressants were discontinued, and the patient was referred to a multidisciplinary sarcoma team, ultimately requiring amputation. ES is a rare soft-tissue neoplasm most commonly affecting the distal extremities of young adults, with peak incidence around the age of 35 years.1It tends to grow along tendons, fascia, and nerves, with differentiation reflected in its varied immunohistochemical findings.2Histologically, ES appears as a dermal or subcutaneous nodule composed of epithelioid and spindle cells, which may be well circumscribed or irregularly lobulated, often with central necrosis. Immunohistochemistry typically shows positive results for cytokeratin and vimentin, with approximately 50% of cases with positive staining for CD34 and 40% showing ERG immunoreactivity.3,4ES is usually negative for S100, desmin, FLI-1, and CD31, although focal CD31 cytoplasmic expression has been described.2,5The highly sensitive diagnostic feature is loss of nuclear SMARCB1/INI1 protein expression.1 Prognosis remains poor due to diagnostic delays, high local recurrence rates, and distant metastasis. Five-year survival ranges from 25% to 70%.1The proximal subtype, typically involving the trunk, pelvis, or proximal limbs, is characterized by larger, pleomorphic cells and follows a more aggressive course.1The more common classic (distal) subtype typically affects the hands and forearms and may initially be less aggressive; however, it can metastasize, and the presence of high-grade histologic features, such as mitoses, necrosis, and atypia, results in behavior resembling the proximal variant. Importantly, ES is often chemoresistant, which explains why radical surgical approaches, including amputation in this case, may be required.1 Clinically, ES initially presents as a painless, firm dermal or subcutaneous nodule. It has been associated with prior trauma and may develop superficial bleeding or necrosis that can become painful.1Rarely, ES manifests as a nonhealing, ulcerative process with raised margins, mimicking conditions like perforating granuloma annulare,Mycobacterium ulcerans, or even PG, as in a case where diagnosis was delayed for 18 years.6Distinguishing features include the histologic absence of palisading granulomas, lack of organisms, and confirmatory immunohistochemical findings. Given the ambiguous presentation of ES, accurate diagnosis requires a high level of suspicion. HFUS has successfully identified ES even when tumors were not palpable or initially missed with magnetic resonance imaging, and it is increasingly used in skin oncology to assess lesion depth and vascularization.7,8Contrary to ES, findings of HFUS for perforating granuloma annulare typically appear as a poorly defined hypoechoic band in the dermis, while active PG demonstrates a heterogeneous, edematous process.9,10When used alongside clinical assessment and dermatopathology, HFUS can help differentiate lesions and assess involvement with nearby structures. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge in distinguishing ES from mimicking ulcers and emphasizes the importance of early imaging and repeat biopsy with immunohistochemical staining to reduce morbidity and guide appropriate treatment.
